title: University of Michigan Drops First-Semester Grades for Freshmen Citing Mental Health Crisis
excerpt: The university's largest college will replace letter grades with pass/no credit for incoming freshmen starting fall 2027, joining a growing number of elite schools rethinking academic pressure.
body:
• University of Michigan's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts will replace letter grades with pass/no credit for all first-semester freshmen starting fall 2027.
  • The policy aims to "curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," though internal letter grades will still be tracked for scholarships and advising.
  • The move affects roughly half of Michigan's 8,000 first-year students; business and engineering colleges are excluded.
  • Critics argue the policy coddles students, while supporters say it follows successful models at MIT, Caltech, and Swarthmore.

The University of Michigan's largest college will stop recording letter grades on transcripts for first-semester freshmen beginning in fall 2027, replacing them with pass or no credit designations in a pilot program aimed at reducing student stress.

The College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, which enrolls about half of Michigan's roughly 8,000 incoming freshmen each year, announced the shift as part of what it called an effort to "curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals."

How the New System Works

Under the new policy, first-semester students will still receive letter grades and instructor feedback on all coursework throughout the semester. However, those grades will not appear on official transcripts and will not factor into students' grade point averages.

Transcripts will instead show a "P" for pass or "NC" for no credit for all first-semester courses. Starting in the second semester, grading reverts to the university's traditional letter-grade system.

"We believe that covering grades will help students start strong and curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals."

— University of Michigan College of LSA

Internal university records will still track the letter grades for academic advising, scholarships, awards, internships, and for students transferring to a major outside the LSA college. A university spokesman declined to comment on how the decision was reached.

Part of a Broader Trend

Michigan joins a growing list of elite institutions that have adopted similar "grade-covering" programs. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has used a pass/no record system for freshmen since 1968, giving students either "pass" or "no record" during their first semester. The California Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College, Johns Hopkins University, Goucher College, and Wellesley College have all implemented comparable policies.

The shift comes as universities across the country grapple with conflicting pressures. Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences voted in May to cap "A" grades at roughly 20% of undergraduate enrollment beginning in fall 2027, a direct response to decades of grade inflation.

Meanwhile, a recent University of California San Diego faculty report found that the percentage of students placed in remedial math classes before they could take precalculus increased to 8.5% in 2025 from 0.5% in 2020, raising concerns about college readiness.

Backlash and Debate

The policy has drawn criticism from those who argue it shields students from accountability. Education commentators have questioned whether removing grade consequences in the first semester addresses the root causes of the mental health crisis or simply delays academic pressure.

University officials counter that the program is designed to help students "acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys." They also say it will foster collaboration over competition and encourage students to explore unfamiliar subjects without fear of damaging their academic records.

Students in Michigan's business and engineering colleges will not be affected by the change.

What It Means for Indian-American Families

The University of Michigan is among the top destinations for Indian-American students and has one of the largest South Asian student populations at any U.S. public university. For diaspora families who often place significant emphasis on academic achievement and GPA-driven outcomes, the shift represents a meaningful change in how first-year academic performance is evaluated.

The policy could ease the transition for students adjusting to the competitive academic environment at a major research university, though some families may worry about how pass/no credit designations on transcripts could affect graduate school applications and early career opportunities.

What's Next

The pilot program will launch with the fall 2027 cohort. The university has not specified how it will evaluate the program's effectiveness or whether it could be expanded to other colleges within the university system. The LSA college, which serves approximately 19,700 undergraduate students, remains the only unit affected for now.
nri_angle: The policy directly affects thousands of Indian-American students and families who make up a significant portion of U-M's undergraduate population, one of the largest groups of international and diaspora students at any U.S. public university.
